summary:
The documented exposure points for transgender travellers in France are detention and the border. In accommodation, services and public movement, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition, and the rights ombudsman has issued formal guidance to service providers in response.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, together with ministry and association input, and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure to strip-searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its own 2010 opinion, notwithstanding the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. In an interview, the national preventive mechanism explained that a new opinion was necessary because the 2010 opinion produced no improvement, the gender-recognition law and terminology had changed, and coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees; it identified structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable people and in suicide prevention, built on a decade of letters from detained trans people.

Placement by birth sex remained the practice in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October, according to 20 Minutes of 4 February 2025. A deputy raised her incarceration as an oral question to the Keeper of the Seals in the National Assembly, arguing that her case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; the placement question remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At the border, the documented friction is document-based and public. The trans woman Giovanna Rincon described, in a first-person account published by StreetPress on 7 March 2017, ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at an airport, questioned in front of other travellers. French law contains no visa, asylum or border-entry provision specific to LGBTQ people, so entry decisions turn on ordinary documentary checks in which a mismatch between presentation and documents can be raised openly.

Transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by imprisonment since 2017, and the law of 31 December 2004 covers injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with penalties increased where an assault or killing is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Enforcement indicators point the other way: a report released on 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults during 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against around 1,380 in 2018. Those are raw counts with no population denominator supplied, so they indicate direction of travel rather than a rate.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming from case files and association testimony that fundamental-rights violations persist, citing the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and setting out official guidance for service providers.

Partner recognition is settled at the baseline: France's marriage-equality law took effect in May 2013, and the country's first same-sex wedding was performed days later. The Court of Cassation ruled in December 2019 that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven and slow. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, and recommended an informed-consent and self-determination model. Gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979, but trans rights organisations stated that the 2010 decree removing gender identity disorder as a diagnosis changed nothing in practice. A visitor needing continuity of treatment should expect the same waiting times and geographic inequity that the report describes for residents.
tangentialFactors:
Official hostility toward trans people surfaces in medical and legislative settings rather than in criminal law. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and a "primarily social problem" and advised extreme caution, though this did not change actual practice. In March 2024 centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all forms of gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender-affirming care, which called such care a "health scandal" and youth transness a "social contagion"; the resulting bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, provoking large-scale protests, but is opposed by the Macron government and has had no update since 23 July 2024.

In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, the interministerial body fighting anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory, which had called gender-affirming healthcare "mutilation"; one committee member resigned and the president stepped away.

Conversion therapy was banned effective 1 February 2022, punishable by two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine; the association Le Refuge estimated that 3–4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy before the ban.

Public opinion is comparatively permissive. A 2013 Pew Research Center survey found 77% of the French population believed homosexuality should be accepted, one of the highest of 39 countries polled, with 81% acceptance among 18–29 year-olds; the 2019 Eurobarometer found 79% backed same-sex marriage and 85% believed LGBT people should have equal rights, and the 2023 Eurobarometer found 79% and 84% respectively. Paris Pride drew 500,000 people in 2019, and pride events now run in dozens of cities nationwide, with Le Marais, Quartier Pigalle and Bois de Boulogne hosting established LGBTQ nightlife.

Acceptance is markedly lower in France's outlying territories: a 2014 study found about 20% of overseas residents saw homosexuality as a sexuality like any other against 77% in metropolitan France, with Mayotte particularly taboo and the first same-sex marriages in Saint Martin and French Polynesia triggering public demonstrations. Mayotte also sees frequent reports of family rejection, harassment and discrimination, and a 2006 Lifou Island proposal for a "family code" envisaged eviction or lynching of LGBTQ people; it was not approved.

The historical baseline is decriminalisation: sodomy was decriminalised in the Penal Code of 1791. A 1960 ordinance doubled penalties for indecent exposure when homosexual in nature and remained in force until 1980, and the Vichy government's 1942 article 334 set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, equalised at 15 in 1982. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 before 1980, still awaiting a Senate vote.
localsOnly:
Transsexualism is covered under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, so residents have a statutory route to funded care alongside the waiting times and geographic inequity documented by ILGA-Europe.

In higher education, Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced in March 2019 that all institutions must use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. At school level, Education Minister Xavier Darcos made fighting discrimination including homophobia one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009, and in January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign Tous égaux, tous alliés, which gives students reporting services and a helpline, requires all French schools to provide guidance about LGBTQ issues, and designates 17 May as a sensitisation day.

Youth care is contested. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for medical care of trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 alongside calcium and vitamin D, while the Senate-passed under-18 transition ban remains pending and opposed by the government.

France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens until 2015, leaving many in legal limbo. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state coverage for women under 43, the MSM blood donation deferral was removed entirely on 16 March 2022, and intersex people retain significant gaps in protection from non-consensual medical interventions.

Homosexuality and cross-dressing were historically treated as immoral, with LGBTQ people facing legal harassment under public morality and order laws; LGBT people may serve openly in the French Armed Forces. The National Assembly voted 293–222 against same-sex marriage in June 2011, and conservative outrage greeted the use of "parent 1" and "parent 2" on French school enrolment forms reported in February 2019. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic and transphobic violence as "unworthy of France" and promised unspecified "concrete measures".

A report released on 16 May 2020 recorded police identifying around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019 against around 1,380 in 2018; these are raw counts without a population denominator.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory states how French authorities treat gender markers on foreign passports or identity documents at entry, or whether a mismatch between a visitor's gender presentation and document sex triggers secondary examination beyond the single 2017 first-person account of public questioning by border police. The general rule governing document checks for arriving visitors is not sourced here.

No source addresses sex-segregated facilities such as hostel or hotel bathrooms, changing rooms or spas as they would apply to a trans visitor. One reported incident from a Lyon hostel in August 2024, sourced to Women's Forum Australia, concerns a dispute in which a manager invoked transphobia against a complaining guest; it does not establish how French law or establishment practice treats a trans guest's access, and remains unresolved on that point.

The 2019 figure of around 1,870 police-identified victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks is a raw count with no denominator and no breakdown separating trans victims from gay and lesbian victims, so it cannot be read as a trans-specific rate.

The inventory contains no figure for trans-specific killings in France against the country's general homicide rate, and none is asserted here; no trans-specific violence magnitude can be derived from the sources provided.

Whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has changed facility-level practice since issuance is not documented in the inventory; the most recent placement case reported, Louna's in February 2025, postdates it.

The status of the Senate bill banning medical transition under 18 has had no update since 23 July 2024 in the sources supplied, and its final disposition is unresolved.
